research.subject: A red kidney bean germinating: one documented growth sequence from the University of Nebraska–Lincoln’s photographic teaching resource, authored by Ellen T. Paparozzi, M. Elizabeth Conley and Christian G. Elowsky. The seeds were grown in perlite; the source does not give calendar dates or a precise growing location. Use the documented sequence as reference for an accelerated 8-second widescreen animation—not as eight seconds of real growth. Suggested staging: 0–2 seconds, water uptake and swelling; 2–4 seconds, root emergence and downward growth; 4–8 seconds, shoot rising toward overhead light. Exact voice-over: “A seed takes in water. Roots grow downward, and a shoot reaches up toward the light.” No on-screen text or music. ([passel2.unl.edu](https://passel2.unl.edu/view/lesson/ecfd27c27b15))

looks.thing: Red kidney bean seed, before germination
looks.look: The source documents a hard outer seed coat and a visible hilum—the scar where the seed was attached to its pod. Inside are two cotyledons, described as a large white mass, and an embryo at the seed’s tip. Do not depict an empty shell containing a separate miniature seed. ([passel2.unl.edu](https://passel2.unl.edu/view/lesson/ecfd27c27b15/5))

The seed coat expands and may begin slipping off, but can remain attached to the growing cotyledons. Avoid making the entire coat instantly disappear when water arrives. ([passel2.unl.edu](https://passel2.unl.edu/view/lesson/ecfd27c27b15/6))

The elongating radicle has become taproot-like, with lateral roots growing from it. This supports a prominent main root with smaller side branches rather than several identical thick roots. The page does not specify root color. ([passel2.unl.edu](https://passel2.unl.edu/view/lesson/ecfd27c27b15/9))

Cotyledons are appearing and the first unifoliate leaves are just peeking out. Magnified photographs show shiny, hair-like trichomes on these leaves. These hairs are a close-up detail, not necessarily appropriate at the animation’s normal scale. ([passel2.unl.edu](https://passel2.unl.edu/view/lesson/ecfd27c27b15/9))

Two unifoliate leaves unfold and expand, revealing the terminal growing apex between them. Use this paired-leaf stage as the endpoint, rather than adding flowers or mature foliage. ([passel2.unl.edu](https://passel2.unl.edu/view/lesson/ecfd27c27b15/12))

UF/IFAS describes horticultural perlite as white, angular, pearl-like pebbles. Perlite—not brown garden soil—was the medium in the documented Nebraska sequence. A cutaway presentation is an animation convention, not a claim about the original apparatus. ([ask.ifas.ufl.edu](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/HS405?utm_source=openai))

facts.fact: The documented episode begins with red kidney beans planted in perlite. The authors explain that perlite supports the seed, permits aeration and makes the roots easy to view. This gives the film a specific observed sequence rather than an invented historical incident. ([passel2.unl.edu](https://passel2.unl.edu/view/lesson/ecfd27c27b15/5))
facts.when: Day 0 after sowing; calendar date and publication date not stated.

facts.fact: During days 1–2, the planted bean absorbs water and its seed coat swells. The coat may begin slipping off, although complete shedding can take days or may not occur. This directly supports the opening voice-over sentence. ([passel2.unl.edu](https://passel2.unl.edu/view/lesson/ecfd27c27b15/6))
facts.when: Days 1–2 after sowing; calendar dates not stated.

facts.fact: The photographic sequence documents the embryonic root, or radicle, emerging from the bean seed on days 3–4. Show root emergence before the above-ground leafy shoot. ([passel2.unl.edu](https://passel2.unl.edu/view/lesson/ecfd27c27b15/7))
facts.when: Days 3–4 after sowing; calendar dates not stated.

facts.fact: The growth timeline records continued radicle growth, root formation and hypocotyl growth during days 4–6. The transformation therefore takes days and must be compressed for an eight-second explainer. ([passel2.unl.edu](https://passel2.unl.edu/revision/lesson/ecfd27c27b15/66405/3))
facts.when: Days 4–6 after sowing; calendar dates not stated.

facts.fact: By days 7–8, lateral roots are growing from the developing taproot, cotyledons are starting to appear and the first unifoliate leaves are peeking out. This provides a documented transition from a sprouted seed to a recognizable seedling. ([passel2.unl.edu](https://passel2.unl.edu/view/lesson/ecfd27c27b15/9))
facts.when: Days 7–8 after sowing; calendar dates not stated.

facts.fact: Around days 11–12, the two unifoliate leaves unfold and expand, exposing the terminal apex. This is the outcome of the selected early-growth episode and a suitable final image. ([passel2.unl.edu](https://passel2.unl.edu/view/lesson/ecfd27c27b15/12))
facts.when: Days 11–12 after sowing; calendar dates not stated.

facts.fact: General biological context, not a separate observation in the bean sequence: roots grow in the direction of gravity, called positive gravitropism; shoots grow away from gravity, called negative gravitropism. Downward root growth should not be presented as simply following a visible beam of light. ([fastplants.org](https://fastplants.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/WFPphysiology-06web.pdf))
facts.when: Undated teaching document; applies during seedling growth.

facts.fact: General biological context: growing shoots can bend toward light through phototropism. The Wisconsin Fast Plants teaching guide distinguishes this response from gravitropism. For the exact narration, overhead illumination can communicate the shoot reaching upward toward light without implying that light alone determines its initial upward direction. ([fastplants.org](https://fastplants.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/WFPphysiology-06web.pdf))
facts.when: Undated teaching document; applies during shoot growth.

story.style: 30-second widescreen live-action macro study with an eight-second simple-animation passage; documentary realism, overhead illumination, no on-screen text or music.
story.story:
For the opening seven seconds, live-action macro photography shows a red kidney bean planted in white, angular, pearl-like perlite; its hard seed coat and visible hilum establish the seed’s appearance. [1]

The next eight seconds compress germination into simple animation. [2–5] The exact voice-over accompanies this sequence: “A seed takes in water. Roots grow downward, and a shoot reaches up toward the light.” [2, 7, 8] On days 1–2, the seed absorbs water and its coat swells rather than instantly disappearing. [2] On days 3–4, the radicle emerges before the leafy shoot. [3] During days 4–6, the radicle lengthens, roots form, and the hypocotyl grows. [4] The root extends downward while the shoot grows upward beneath overhead illumination. [7, 8] By days 7–8, smaller lateral roots branch from the main root, cotyledons appear, and the first unifoliate leaves peek out. [5]

The final fifteen seconds return to live-action time-lapse of days 11–12: two unifoliate leaves unfold and expand, exposing the terminal apex between them. [6] This paired-leaf seedling is the final image. [6]
